summary:
The United Kingdom enforces single-sex facilities on the basis of biological sex. A code from the national equality body came into force in August 2026. It gives organisations practical examples for compliance in toilets, changing rooms and similar spaces.

On 19 June 2026 a judge in the Court of Session, Lady Ross, held that guidance from the Scottish Prison Service on custody of trans prisoners was unlawful. The guidance had allowed some trans prisoners to be held in jails matching gender identity rather than sex at birth. The court held that sex segregation in prisons must rest on a lawful basis.

British Transport Police adopted an interim position after the Supreme Court ruling on sex. Trans women are to be strip-searched by officers of their sex at birth. The prior policy had permitted trans women staff to intimately search women even where the staff member held a Gender Recognition Certificate.

Police Scotland published interim guidance on 25 June 2025 for searching transgender persons. Searches in custody and under stop-and-search that involve removal of more than a jacket, gloves, headgear or footwear are conducted on the basis of biological sex. Where lived gender differs, efforts will be made on request to provide an officer of the lived gender.

Since December 2023 the United Kingdom no longer accepts gender recognition certificates issued by 50 foreign countries and United States states, including Sweden, New York State and Belgium, on the ground that those systems permit transition too easily. Holders from those places must apply for a new certificate under British law to obtain gender recognition in the United Kingdom.

Same-sex marriage is recognised throughout the United Kingdom. It took effect in England and Wales on 13 March 2014 under the Marriage (Same Sex Couples) Act 2013, in Scotland in 2014, and in Northern Ireland on 13 January 2020 following intervention by the United Kingdom Parliament.

The TransActual Gendered Spaces Report 2025 recorded fears of harassment in public gendered spaces among trans, intersex and gender-nonconforming respondents. Respondents linked the fear to opposition to their inclusion.

On 18 August 2026 United Nations human rights experts warned that revisions to the Equality Act 2010 risk discriminating against and excluding transgender people.
tangentialFactors:
The February 2026 hearing in the Scottish prison case presented opposing positions. Counsel argued that housing trans prisoners by sex at birth would breach human rights and create an unacceptable suicide risk. Government lawyers defended the guidance that limited the women’s estate to biological females with individual risk assessments as flexible.

Legal commentary published on 16 July 2026 analysed the 19 June ruling through Schedule 22(1) of the Equality Act 2010, the Prison Rules, the Gender Recognition Act 2004 and the court’s approach to Article 8.

Northern Ireland operates under different equality legislation and was still assessing the impact of the Supreme Court ruling at the time of the August 2026 code. The code was welcomed by the campaign group Sex Matters, whose representative Maya Forstater described the law as clear and the code as practical.

The minister for Women and Equalities described the December 2023 decision to refuse certain foreign certificates as long overdue. The opposition equalities spokesperson warned of diplomatic consequences because the refusal list excluded Canada, the United States, Australia and New Zealand.

Press coverage of trans people has been described as increasing and more vitriolic since 2016 and as super-charged since 2018. A 2019 study by Paul Baker found numerous 2018 and 2019 press articles that were critical of trans people and cast them as unreasonable and aggressive.

ILGA-Europe recorded a fall for the United Kingdom from first in Europe with 86 percent in 2015 to ninth in 2020 with 66 percent and 22nd in 2025 with 45 percent, the third steepest drop from 2024. Its leadership cited a hostile climate on trans rights fuelled by opposition groups.
localsOnly:
Since 4 April 2005 transgender people may apply to the Gender Recognition Panel for a Gender Recognition Certificate after two years living in the acquired gender, without mandatory sex reassignment surgery. A certificate permits a new birth certificate and full legal recognition of acquired sex for all purposes. The route followed Goodwin v United Kingdom (2002), which found a breach of Articles 8 and 12 after Corbett v Corbett (1970) had prevented changes to birth certificate sex markers.

A married applicant was originally required to divorce or annul the marriage before a certificate could issue, followed by dissolution, recognition and registration of a civil partnership with associated paperwork and costs. Under current law a certificate will not issue unless the spouse consents. If consent is refused the marriage must be terminated.

Medical gender reassignment is formally approved and available through the National Health Service or privately. A December 2002 government policy document states that transsexualism is not a mental illness. European anti-discrimination law on gender was held to apply to trans people in P v S and Cornwall County Council (1996).

NHS England stated in March 2024 that gender identity clinics would stop prescribing puberty blockers to children and young people. The stop was renewed indefinitely in December 2024 for reconsideration in 2027. Reporting in April 2025 stated that no new prescriptions of gender-affirming hormones had been issued to minors in the year since the Cass Review, with some families turning to black-market or overseas hormones.

The Cass Review in April 2024 led to closure of the Tavistock Gender Identity Development Service in March 2024. Only two of eight planned regional centres had opened, and many 16- and 17-year-olds were transferred to adult services. In Bell v Tavistock in December 2020 the court found children under 16 could not independently consent to puberty blockers. That finding was overturned on appeal in September 2021.

In January 2022 the Girls’ Day School Trust barred admission of trans girls without a Gender Recognition Certificate. In July 2022 the Rugby Football Union and Rugby Football League adopted single-sex participation rules for under-12s that excluded trans girls from girls’ teams.

Civil partnerships have been available since 2005 and confer most but not all rights of marriage, with recognition problems reported in other countries.
outOfScopeNotes:
The searching and biological-sex policy of Surrey Police, released under the Freedom of Information Act, was not retrievable at research time. Its content remains unresolved because access returned HTTP 403.

Societal acceptance of transgender people specifically remains not sourced. The inventory contains only sexuality-specific tolerance figures, 86 percent agreeing homosexuality should be accepted in a 2019 poll and 77 percent supporting same-sex marriage in a 2017 poll, which do not measure trans acceptance.

The full TransActual Gendered Spaces Report 2025 was published as a PDF. Findings beyond the surveyed fear of harassment in gendered spaces were not extracted in the inventory and remain not sourced here.
